title: Κώνωψ καὶ ταῦρος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 189. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κώνωψ ἐπιστὰς κέρατι ταύρου καὶ πολὺν χρόνον ἐπικαθίσας, ἐπειδὴ ἀπαλλάττεσθαι ἔμελλεν, ἐπυνθάνετο τοῦ ταύρου εἰ ἤδη βούλεται αὐτὸν ἀπελθεῖν.
sentences.tr: Kōnōps epistas kerati taurou kai polyn chronon epikathisas, epeidē apallattesthai emellen, epynthaneto tou taurou ei ēdē bouletai auton apelthein.
sentences.l: A gnat, having taken his stand on a bull's horn and having sat there a long time, when he was about to take himself off, inquired of the bull whether he now wished him to go away.
sentences.i: A gnat settled on a bull's horn, sat there a long while, and, when he meant to be off, asked the bull whether he would like him to go now.
sentences.n: πυνθάνομαι takes the genitive of the person asked, τοῦ ταύρου. The indirect question keeps the tense the gnat actually used — βούλεται stays present after a past main verb, where English shifts it back to "wished". πολὺν χρόνον is the accusative of duration.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ὑποτυχὼν εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ οὔτε, ὅτε ἦλθες, ἔγνων, οὔτε, ἐὰν ἀπέλθῃς, γνώσομαι. »
sentences.tr: Ho de hypotychōn eipen· « All’ oute, hote ēlthes, egnōn, oute, ean apelthēis, gnōsomai. »
sentences.l: And he, taking-up-the-word, said: « Why, neither when you came did I know it, nor, if you go away, shall I know it. »
sentences.i: And the bull answered: « Why, I never noticed you come, and I shall not notice you go. »
sentences.n: ὑποτυχών is the collection's regular "taking up the word", to answer — there is no seizing in it. ἀλλά opening a reply is dismissive, near English "why,…". γιγνώσκω here is to become aware of a thing, not to know it already. The two limbs are deliberately unlike: ὅτε with the aorist for what did happen, ἐάν with the subjunctive for what may.

sentences.t: Τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ χρήσαιτο ἄν τις πρὸς ἄνδρα ἀδύνατον, ὃς οὔτε παρὼν οὔτε ἀπὼν ἐπιβλαβὴς ἢ ὠφέλιμός ἐστι.
sentences.tr: Toutōi tōi logōi chrēsaito an tis pros andra adynaton, hos oute parōn oute apōn epiblabēs ē ōphelimos esti.
sentences.l: This story someone might use against a powerless man, who neither when present nor when absent is harmful or useful.
sentences.i: One might use this story against an ineffectual man, who whether he is there or not does neither harm nor good.
sentences.n: χρήσαιτο ἄν is the potential optative, the standing form of this closing; χράομαι takes the dative of what is used. ἀδύνατος is not weak so much as incapable of effect — the point of the fable. παρών and ἀπών are participles doing the work of English clauses.
